text: Most teams meet performance work for the first time through a user complaint or an incident. At that point, whoever's on call is debugging a production slowdown under time pressure, with incomplete data, while the business impact is already happening. That's an incident response with extra steps, not a performance practice — and this lesson is about the alternative.

Performance engineering as a discipline means the opposite posture: measuring, profiling, and improving performance as planned, ongoing engineering work. A regression gets caught in a pull request or a nightly benchmark, long before it ever reaches a real user, instead of after it's already costing the business something.

When something's slow, intuition reaches for a guess — it's probably the database, it's probably serialization. Sometimes that's right. Often it isn't, and the fix built on that guess makes no measurable difference because it was never the actual bottleneck. Profiling replaces the guess with evidence: a flame graph shows exactly where time is spent across the full call stack, and distributed tracing does the same thing across service boundaries. Profile first, then fix what the profile actually shows.

The core method fits in one sentence: establish a real baseline, change exactly one thing, measure again under the same conditions before concluding anything. Skip the baseline and you can't tell if a change helped. Change more than one thing at once and even an improved number doesn't tell you which change caused it — a harmful change could be canceling out a helpful one while both still exist in production.

A performance budget makes this continuous: a defined, enforceable limit on latency or resource cost, checked automatically in CI on every change. That turns 'did this slow things down' into a gate code has to pass, not a question asked after a slow release has already shipped — catching the regression as a changed line of code instead of an incident. Next lesson applies all of this to a spike you can actually see coming.
